definitions.text: Exhausted; completely worn out.
Of an object: broken beyond repair. The washing machine's knackered.

examples.text: I'm absolutely knackered, I've been up since five.
examples.translation: I'm completely exhausted, I've been awake since five.
examples.context: The most frequent use by far.

examples.text: Don't bother with that laptop, it's knackered.
examples.translation: Don't bother with that laptop, it's beyond saving.

origin.etymology: A knacker bought worn-out horses for slaughter, and the knacker's yard was where they ended up. A knackered horse was one fit only for that trip — the metaphor has outlived the trade by a century.

definitions.text: Extremely tired. Slightly milder in tone than knackered and safe in any company.

examples.text: I was shattered after the flight.
examples.translation: I was worn out after the flight.

examples.text: She looked shattered by the end of the shift.
examples.translation: She looked exhausted by the end of the shift.

definitions.text: Bitterly disappointed. Used for losses that genuinely hurt — a job you didn't get, a match your team lost — and, ironically, for very small ones.

examples.text: He was gutted when they didn't pick him for the squad.
examples.translation: He was devastated when they left him out of the squad.

examples.text: They'd sold the last one. Gutted.
examples.translation: They'd sold the last one. Gutting.
examples.context: Standing alone as a one-word reaction — very common, and usually lightly ironic.

origin.etymology: From gutting a fish: everything inside removed. The word is a fixture of post-match football interviews, which is largely how it spread from regional use to national.

definitions.text: Pleased, delighted — usually about something you had a hand in. Often intensified as chuffed to bits.

examples.text: She was dead chuffed with her exam results.
examples.translation: She was really pleased with her exam results.

examples.text: I'm chuffed to bits for you, honestly.
examples.translation: I'm genuinely delighted for you.

origin.etymology: From dialect chuff, 'plump, pleased'. Confusingly, an obsolete second sense of chuffed meant displeased — the two coexisted for a while before the positive one won outright.

definitions.text: Overjoyed. Strongly associated with Liverpool and the North West, though understood nationally.

examples.text: I'm made up you could come.
examples.translation: I'm so pleased you could come.

examples.text: He was made up when the baby arrived.
examples.translation: He was overjoyed when the baby was born.

definitions.text: Impertinent in a way that is more amusing than offensive.
Of an indulgence: small, unplanned and mildly naughty. A cheeky pint, a cheeky takeaway.
definitions.note: This second sense is now the more common one, and it attaches to almost any treat.

examples.text: Don't be cheeky to your gran.
examples.translation: Don't be impertinent to your grandmother.
examples.context: The original sense, mostly said to children.

examples.text: Fancy a cheeky pint after work?
examples.translation: Fancy a quick unplanned pint after work?
examples.context: Nothing rude is implied — cheeky here just means 'slightly indulgent'.

definitions.text: Suspicious, untrustworthy, probably illegal.
Unreliable or in poor condition. A dodgy knee, a dodgy connection.
Of food: likely to make you ill.

examples.text: He got it off some dodgy bloke down the market.
examples.translation: He bought it from some shady man at the market.

examples.text: The wifi's been dodgy all morning.
examples.translation: The wifi has been unreliable all morning.

examples.text: I think that prawn sandwich was a bit dodgy.
examples.translation: I think that prawn sandwich was off.

definitions.text: Pointless fuss and bother; unnecessary hassle. As a noun: it's a bit of a faff.
To dither, to busy oneself unproductively. Usually faff about or faff around.

examples.text: Parking there is a total faff, get the train.
examples.translation: Parking there is far more hassle than it's worth, take the train.

examples.text: Stop faffing about and get in the car.
examples.translation: Stop dithering and get in the car.

definitions.text: A man; a guy. Completely neutral, and the default word for an unnamed male.

examples.text: Some bloke came round asking about the car.
examples.translation: Some man came by asking about the car.

examples.text: He's a decent bloke, you'll like him.
examples.translation: He's a good sort, you'll get on with him.

origin.etymology: Of uncertain origin — proposals include Shelta (Irish Traveller cant) and Dutch blok. It surfaced in mid-19th-century English and has stayed resolutely ordinary ever since.

definitions.text: A man, with a distinctly London flavour — often implying a certain streetwise swagger. A proper geezer is a compliment.

examples.text: Ask that geezer behind the bar.
examples.translation: Ask that man behind the bar.

examples.text: Dave? He's a proper geezer.
examples.translation: Dave? He's a real character, salt of the earth.

origin.etymology: From dialect guiser, a mummer or someone in disguise. Note the transatlantic split: in American English geezer means an old man, which it does not mean in Britain.

definitions.text: A friend. The most common word for one in British English.
Used to address any man, friend or stranger. Cheers, mate.
Said flatly to a stranger who has annoyed you, it is a warning rather than a friendly greeting.
definitions.note: Tone is everything. 'Alright, mate?' and 'Mate.' are not the same speech act.

examples.text: I'm meeting a few mates for a drink.
examples.translation: I'm meeting some friends for a drink.

examples.text: Cheers, mate, appreciate it.
examples.translation: Thanks, pal, I appreciate it.

examples.text: Mate. That's my seat.
examples.translation: Excuse me. That's my seat.
examples.context: Clipped and flat. This is confrontational.

definitions.text: A boy or young man.
The lads: a man's group of male friends, particularly in a going-out context.
A man given to drinking and boisterousness — sometimes admiring, sometimes not.
definitions.note: The adjective laddish is almost always critical.

examples.text: He's a good lad, always helps out.
examples.translation: He's a good young man, always helps out.

examples.text: Out with the lads on Saturday.
examples.translation: Out with my mates on Saturday.

definitions.text: Tacky, in poor taste, unfashionable. Aimed squarely at things that are trying and failing to be impressive.

examples.text: The hotel was nice but the decor was a bit naff.
examples.translation: The hotel was nice but the decor was rather tacky.

examples.text: That's a naff excuse and you know it.
examples.translation: That's a feeble excuse and you know it.

origin.etymology: Origin genuinely uncertain. It was current in Polari, the coded slang of gay and theatrical circles in mid-century Britain, and broke into general use in the 1970s. The various acronym explanations circulating online are backronyms with no evidence behind them.

definitions.text: Disgusting; foul-smelling or filthy.
Of a person: unattractive. This use is unkind and increasingly avoided.

examples.text: That bin's been out a week, it's minging.
examples.translation: That bin's been out for a week, it's revolting.

examples.text: The weather was minging all weekend.
examples.translation: The weather was miserable all weekend.

origin.etymology: From Scots ming, 'a bad smell'. It spread south in the 1990s. The 'ugly' sense is a later extension and is the reason the word now carries a caution.

definitions.text: Disgusting, especially in taste or smell.

examples.text: That energy drink is absolutely rank.
examples.translation: That energy drink tastes revolting.

examples.text: The changing rooms smelled rank.
examples.translation: The changing rooms smelled foul.

definitions.text: Bleak, unpleasant, thoroughly bad. Applied to weather, places, moods and situations with equal ease.
Of a person: feeling ill or very low. I felt grim all day.

examples.text: February in Manchester is pretty grim.
examples.translation: February in Manchester is fairly bleak.

examples.text: I felt grim after that curry.
examples.translation: I felt awful after that curry.

definitions.text: Of a person: reliable, decent, good company. He's sound.
Fine; no problem. Used alone as an acknowledgement.

examples.text: Ask Jen, she's sound, she'll help you out.
examples.translation: Ask Jen, she's a good sort, she'll help you.

examples.text: —I'll be ten minutes late. —Sound.
examples.translation: 'I'll be ten minutes late.' 'No problem.'

definitions.text: Excellent, brilliant. Strongest in the North of England and Scotland.

examples.text: That gig was mint.
examples.translation: That gig was brilliant.

examples.text: Your new bike's mint, mate.
examples.translation: Your new bike's great, mate.

origin.etymology: From mint condition — an item so unworn it might have just left the mint. The adjective broke free of the phrase and now works on its own.

definitions.text: Thrilled, elated, full of anticipation.
Of a place: lively, full of atmosphere.

examples.text: I'm buzzing for the weekend.
examples.translation: I'm really excited about the weekend.

examples.text: Town was buzzing on Saturday night.
examples.translation: The town centre was lively on Saturday night.

definitions.text: Attractive; also, of food, delicious.

examples.text: That chicken shop is peng, honestly.
examples.translation: That chicken shop is genuinely delicious.

examples.text: She looked peng in that photo.
examples.translation: She looked gorgeous in that photo.

origin.etymology: From Multicultural London English, with roots in Jamaican Patois. Like much MLE vocabulary it spread nationally through UK rap and drill, and is strongly generation-marked — mostly used by people under about thirty.

definitions.text: A lot of; loads of. Counter-intuitively, it means the opposite of standard 'bare'.
Very, as an intensifier: it's bare cold.

examples.text: There were bare people outside the station.
examples.translation: There were loads of people outside the station.

examples.text: It's bare long, that journey.
examples.translation: That journey takes ages.

origin.etymology: Multicultural London English. The inversion of the standard meaning is the reason it reliably confuses older speakers, and part of why it caught on.

definitions.text: Thanks; cool; understood. A general-purpose acknowledgement.
Used as a greeting or a farewell on its own.
Of a person: trustworthy, decent.

examples.text: —I'll send it over tonight. —Safe.
examples.translation: 'I'll send it over tonight.' 'Cheers.'

examples.text: Safe, bruv, see you later.
examples.translation: See you, mate, catch you later.

definitions.text: Contraction of 'isn't it', used as a tag on any statement regardless of the grammar of the sentence it follows.
Standing alone: an emphatic agreement, roughly 'exactly'.

examples.text: It's freezing out, innit.
examples.translation: It's freezing out, isn't it.

examples.text: You went all that way for nothing, innit.
examples.translation: You went all that way for nothing, didn't you.
examples.context: Grammatically the tag should be 'didn't you'. innit has replaced the whole system of tag questions for many speakers.

examples.text: —Prices have gone mad. —Innit.
examples.translation: 'Prices have gone mad.' 'Tell me about it.'

definitions.text: Very, really. As an intensifier before an adjective: proper cold, proper good.
Genuine, the real thing. A proper pub, a proper cup of tea.

examples.text: It was proper cold on the platform.
examples.translation: It was really cold on the platform.

examples.text: Now that's a proper breakfast.
examples.translation: Now that's a real breakfast.

definitions.text: Very, extremely. An intensifier with no connection to the literal sense: dead good, dead easy.

examples.text: The recipe's dead easy, takes ten minutes.
examples.translation: The recipe's really easy, it takes ten minutes.

examples.text: She was dead pleased with it.
examples.translation: She was very pleased with it.

definitions.text: A pound sterling. The plural is also quid, never quids: fifty quid.

examples.text: It cost me twenty quid.
examples.translation: It cost me twenty pounds.

examples.text: Have you got a quid for the trolley?
examples.translation: Have you got a pound coin for the trolley?

origin.etymology: In use since the 17th century, origin unsettled. The likeliest account points to Latin quid ('what', as in quid pro quo) passing into cant as a word for the necessary consideration.

definitions.text: A ten-pound note, or the sum of ten pounds. Its companion fiver works the same way.

examples.text: Lend us a tenner till Friday.
examples.translation: Lend me ten pounds until Friday.

examples.text: I found a tenner in my coat pocket.
examples.translation: I found a ten-pound note in my coat pocket.

definitions.text: Broke; having no money at all, usually temporarily.

examples.text: Can't come out, I'm skint till payday.
examples.translation: I can't come out, I'm broke until payday.

examples.text: We were completely skint that first year.
examples.translation: We had no money at all that first year.

origin.etymology: A worn-down form of skinned — stripped of everything, as an animal is skinned.

definitions.text: Money, cash. Slightly dated now — it peaked in the 1980s and 90s.

examples.text: He's made a fair bit of dosh out of it.
examples.translation: He's made a decent amount of money out of it.

examples.text: Bring some dosh, the place is cash only.
examples.translation: Bring some cash, the place doesn't take cards.

definitions.text: A cup of tea. Tea is assumed unless stated otherwise.

examples.text: Sit down, I'll put the kettle on for a cuppa.
examples.translation: Sit down, I'll make you a cup of tea.

examples.text: Nothing a cuppa won't fix.
examples.translation: Nothing a cup of tea won't sort out.
examples.context: Offering tea is the standard British response to distress of any magnitude.

definitions.text: A hot drink, usually tea. Northern England's preferred term where the South says cuppa.

examples.text: Fancy a brew?
examples.translation: Would you like a cup of tea?

examples.text: I'll stick the kettle on, get a brew going.
examples.translation: I'll put the kettle on and make some tea.

definitions.text: A fish and chip shop.
As an adjective: touchy, quick to take offence. An unrelated sense, but a common one.

examples.text: We got chips from the chippy on the way home.
examples.translation: We got chips from the fish and chip shop on the way home.

examples.text: He gets a bit chippy if you mention it.
examples.translation: He gets rather defensive if you bring it up.

definitions.text: A sandwich, particularly a filled roll. A chip butty — chips in buttered bread — is the canonical example.

examples.text: A bacon butty and a brew, please.
examples.translation: A bacon sandwich and a cup of tea, please.

examples.text: You've never had a chip butty?
examples.translation: You've never had a chip sandwich?

origin.etymology: From butter — bread with butter on it. The North of England and Wales say butty, other regions say sarnie or barm, and the national argument over what to call a bread roll is genuinely unresolved.

definitions.text: Food; a meal. Common in the North of England, Scotland and among sailors and soldiers.

examples.text: Right, who's sorting the scran?
examples.translation: Right, who's organising the food?

examples.text: Proper good scran in that pub.
examples.translation: Really good food in that pub.

definitions.text: Drunk. Note the transatlantic trap: in American English pissed means angry. British 'pissed off' means angry; plain 'pissed' does not.

examples.text: He got absolutely pissed at the wedding.
examples.translation: He got completely drunk at the wedding.

examples.text: I'm pissed off with the whole thing.
examples.translation: I'm fed up with the whole thing.
examples.context: With 'off' the meaning flips to annoyance.

definitions.text: So drunk as to be unable to walk properly.

examples.text: She was legless by nine o'clock.
examples.translation: She was completely drunk by nine o'clock.

examples.text: They came back from the pub legless.
examples.translation: They came back from the pub barely able to stand.

definitions.text: Out drinking heavily, as a deliberate plan for the evening.

examples.text: The lads are on the lash tonight.
examples.translation: The lads are out drinking tonight.

examples.text: I can't, I was on the lash last night.
examples.translation: I can't, I was out drinking last night.

definitions.text: A house or flat; someone's place. Round my gaff.

examples.text: We're all going back to his gaff after.
examples.translation: We're all going back to his place afterwards.

examples.text: Nice gaff you've got here.
examples.translation: Nice place you've got here.

definitions.text: A sleep or nap: have a kip.
To sleep, especially somewhere improvised: kip on the sofa.

examples.text: I'm going to have a quick kip before we go out.
examples.translation: I'm going to have a short nap before we go out.

examples.text: You can kip on the sofa if you miss the last train.
examples.translation: You can sleep on the sofa if you miss the last train.

origin.etymology: From Danish kippe, a cheap inn or doss-house. The place-word became the activity.

definitions.text: To laze around doing nothing. Usually doss about.
Something requiring no effort at all: the exam was a doss.

examples.text: We just dossed about all afternoon.
examples.translation: We just lazed around all afternoon.

examples.text: First year was a complete doss.
examples.translation: First year required almost no work at all.

definitions.text: To avoid work or school by slipping away; to shirk. Often skive off.

examples.text: He skived off school for the whole afternoon.
examples.translation: He bunked off school for the whole afternoon.

examples.text: Working from home is not an excuse to skive.
examples.translation: Working from home is not an excuse to shirk.

origin.etymology: Entered English through soldiers in the First World War, plausibly from French esquiver, 'to dodge'.

definitions.text: To steal, usually something small.
To arrest. Get nicked.
As a noun: a police station, or prison. Down the nick.
In good nick / in bad nick: in good or poor condition.
definitions.note: Four unrelated senses sharing one form. Context always disambiguates.

examples.text: Someone's nicked my charger.
examples.translation: Someone's stolen my charger.

examples.text: He got nicked for driving without insurance.
examples.translation: He got arrested for driving without insurance.

examples.text: The car's old but it's in decent nick.
examples.translation: The car's old but it's in good condition.

definitions.text: An informer; someone who reports others to the authorities.
To inform on someone. Usually grass someone up.

examples.text: Nobody likes a grass.
examples.translation: Nobody likes an informer.

examples.text: She grassed him up to the manager.
examples.translation: She reported him to the manager.

origin.etymology: Most often traced to rhyming slang — grasshopper for 'copper' — though the chain is disputed and the word may simply come from the idea of a snake in the grass.

definitions.text: Playful mutual teasing; the good-natured insult trading that holds British friendships together.
Invoked defensively to excuse something that has landed badly: it was only banter.
definitions.note: This second use has made the word contentious — it is now the standard cover for a remark the speaker doesn't want to own.

examples.text: There's good banter in that office.
examples.translation: There's a good atmosphere of joking in that office.

examples.text: Relax, it's just banter.
examples.translation: Relax, I was only joking.
examples.context: Frequently a warning sign rather than a reassurance.

definitions.text: Mocking someone; making fun of them.
Being unreasonable or taking advantage. Forty pounds for that? They're taking the mickey.

examples.text: Are you taking the mickey out of my accent?
examples.translation: Are you making fun of my accent?

examples.text: Six quid for a coffee — they're taking the mickey.
examples.translation: Six pounds for a coffee — that's daylight robbery.

origin.etymology: A sanitised version of a cruder phrase; mickey is a euphemistic substitution. The polite form is now far more common than the original.

definitions.text: A deliberate attempt to provoke or fool someone; a prank. Is this a wind-up?
As a verb, wind someone up: to irritate them on purpose, or to string them along.

examples.text: Tell me you're joking — is this a wind-up?
examples.translation: Tell me you're joking — are you having me on?

examples.text: He knows exactly how to wind his sister up.
examples.translation: He knows exactly how to provoke his sister.

origin.etymology: From winding a clockwork mechanism tighter and tighter until something gives.

definitions.text: An unpleasant or contemptible person. Mild as insults go, and frequently affectionate when prefixed: you lucky git, you daft git.

examples.text: The miserable old git wouldn't even let us park.
examples.translation: The miserable old man wouldn't even let us park.

examples.text: You jammy git, how did you manage that?
examples.translation: You lucky devil, how did you pull that off?

definitions.text: An idiot. Mild, slightly old-fashioned, and more exasperated than aggressive.

examples.text: I felt like a right pillock standing there.
examples.translation: I felt like a complete idiot standing there.

examples.text: Some pillock parked across the drive.
examples.translation: Some fool parked across the driveway.

definitions.text: A fool. Affectionate and dated, carried into general use by 1980s television.

examples.text: You've put it in upside down, you plonker.
examples.translation: You've put it in upside down, you idiot.

examples.text: What a plonker, he's locked himself out again.
examples.translation: What a fool, he's locked himself out again.

definitions.text: An incompetent fool. Implies not malice but a total absence of thought.

examples.text: Some muppet's left the freezer door open.
examples.translation: Some idiot has left the freezer door open.

examples.text: I'm such a muppet, I've booked the wrong date.
examples.translation: I'm such an idiot, I've booked the wrong date.

origin.etymology: From the puppets of the television series — the image is of someone whose strings are being pulled by someone else. It became general British insult vocabulary in the 1990s.

definitions.text: A foolish or hapless person. Scottish in origin, now widely used across Britain, and notably good-humoured for an insult.

examples.text: Don't be a numpty, read the instructions.
examples.translation: Don't be daft, read the instructions.

examples.text: Some numpty's blocked the fire exit.
examples.translation: Some fool has blocked the fire exit.

definitions.text: Astounded; struck speechless with surprise.

examples.text: I was gobsmacked when they announced the winner.
examples.translation: I was astonished when they announced the winner.

examples.text: She looked absolutely gobsmacked.
examples.translation: She looked completely stunned.

origin.etymology: From gob, dialect for 'mouth', plus smacked — the image is of being hit in the mouth, or of clapping a hand over it in shock. Northern English and Scottish in origin, national since the 1980s.

definitions.text: An exclamation of surprise. Dated but still in genuine use, particularly by older speakers.

examples.text: Blimey, that was quick.
examples.translation: Goodness, that was fast.

examples.text: Blimey, have you seen the price of that?
examples.translation: Good grief, have you seen how much that costs?

origin.etymology: Contracted from 'God blind me' — a minced oath that wore down until nothing of the original was recognisable. Cor blimey is the fuller form.

definitions.text: A general-purpose intensifier expressing annoyance, emphasis or admiration: bloody hell, bloody brilliant, bloody typical.

examples.text: It's bloody freezing out there.
examples.translation: It's absolutely freezing out there.

examples.text: Bloody hell, look at that queue.
examples.translation: Good grief, look at that queue.

examples.text: That was a bloody good meal.
examples.translation: That was a really good meal.
examples.context: Positive. The word takes its charge from what surrounds it.

origin.etymology: Considered genuinely shocking in print until the mid-20th century — Shaw's Pygmalion caused a scandal with a single use of it in 1914. It is now near the bottom of the offensiveness scale and functions mostly as emphasis.

definitions.text: Nonsense, rubbish. That's complete bollocks.
As an exclamation of frustration or flat disagreement.
The dog's bollocks: excellent, the very best. The same word with the opposite valence.
definitions.note: A useful illustration of how far context overrides literal meaning in British profanity.

examples.text: He's talking absolute bollocks.
examples.translation: He's talking complete nonsense.

examples.text: Oh bollocks, I've left my keys inside.
examples.translation: Oh damn, I've left my keys inside.

examples.text: Their new album is the dog's bollocks.
examples.translation: Their new album is superb.

definitions.text: Dealt with; arranged. That's the tickets sorted.
As a one-word confirmation that a matter is closed.
Of a person: settled, organised, having their life in order.

examples.text: Don't worry about the booking, it's sorted.
examples.translation: Don't worry about the booking, it's taken care of.

examples.text: —I'll pick you up at seven. —Sorted.
examples.translation: 'I'll pick you up at seven.' 'Perfect.'

definitions.text: Thanks. By far its most common use in Britain — far more often than as a toast.
Goodbye. Frequently both at once, ending a transaction: cheers, bye.
A drinking toast, its original sense.

examples.text: Cheers for sorting that out.
examples.translation: Thanks for sorting that out.

examples.text: Cheers then, see you Monday.
examples.translation: Bye then, see you Monday.

definitions.text: Thanks. Very casual and very short — for small favours, not large ones.

examples.text: Ta, just pop it on the side.
examples.translation: Thanks, just leave it on the counter.

examples.text: Ta very much.
examples.translation: Thanks very much.

origin.etymology: Often described as a child's reduction of 'thank you', and recorded in English since the 18th century.

definitions.text: Physically attractive. Nothing to do with physical fitness, which regularly confuses American and Australian visitors.

examples.text: His brother's quite fit, actually.
examples.translation: His brother is rather good-looking, actually.

examples.text: She thinks the new barista is fit.
examples.translation: She thinks the new barista is attractive.

definitions.text: To be attracted to someone. I think she fancies you.
To want or feel like something. Fancy a pint? — this is the more frequent sense by a distance.

examples.text: Fancy a walk before it gets dark?
examples.translation: Would you like to go for a walk before dark?

examples.text: He's fancied her since university.
examples.translation: He's had a crush on her since university.

definitions.text: To kiss passionately; a prolonged kiss. Slightly adolescent in flavour.

examples.text: They were snogging on the night bus.
examples.translation: They were kissing on the night bus.

examples.text: He's never got over that snog at the Christmas party.
examples.translation: He's never got over that kiss at the Christmas party.

definitions.text: To successfully attract a romantic or sexual partner on a night out.
On the pull: out specifically with that intention.

examples.text: He's wearing his good shirt, he's hoping to pull.
examples.translation: He's wearing his good shirt, he's hoping to meet someone.

examples.text: They were out on the pull all weekend.
examples.translation: They spent the weekend out looking to meet people.

definitions.text: To run, especially to run away in a hurry.

examples.text: We had to leg it for the last train.
examples.translation: We had to sprint for the last train.

examples.text: He legged it as soon as he saw the warden.
examples.translation: He bolted as soon as he saw the warden.

definitions.text: Nerve, courage. He didn't have the bottle to ask.
To bottle it: to lose one's nerve at the decisive moment.

examples.text: It took some bottle to stand up and say that.
examples.translation: It took real courage to stand up and say that.

examples.text: He bottled it on the penalty.
examples.translation: He lost his nerve taking the penalty.

origin.etymology: Usually traced to rhyming slang. The reversal is neat: to have bottle is to be brave, but to bottle it is to be a coward.

definitions.text: Sulky, moody, in a strop. Strongly associated with the East Midlands and Yorkshire.

examples.text: He's been mardy all morning.
examples.translation: He's been sulking all morning.

examples.text: Don't go all mardy on me.
examples.translation: Don't start sulking at me.

origin.etymology: From dialect marred, 'spoiled' — a mardy child was a spoiled one. It reached a wider audience through Northern pop music in the 2000s.

definitions.text: Small, little. In Scotland and Northern Ireland it is not slang so much as the ordinary word, and it is often affectionate rather than literally about size.

examples.text: Give me a wee minute.
examples.translation: Give me a moment.
examples.context: Nothing here is actually small. wee softens the request.

examples.text: We stopped at a wee café by the loch.
examples.translation: We stopped at a little café by the loch.

definitions.text: In the North East of England: good, pleasant, considerable. A canny lad is a nice bloke; canny good means very good.
In standard English and in Scotland: shrewd, cautious. A different word entirely in practice.
definitions.note: The two senses are genuinely separate, and the regional one surprises outsiders.

examples.text: He's a canny lad, you'll get on.
examples.translation: He's a good bloke, you'll get along.

examples.text: There was a canny few people there.
examples.translation: There were quite a lot of people there.
